rejected.title: Budj Bim and Gunditjmara aquaculture
card: Budj Bim is in western Victoria, on Gunditjmara Country. A volcano there erupted long ago and sent lava flows across the land.
The Gunditjmara shaped these lava flows and wetlands. They built channels, weirs and traps to move water and catch shortfin eels.
This system was a form of aquaculture, which means farming water animals. It let people hold and harvest eels in a planned way over thousands of years.
The Budj Bim Cultural Landscape was World Heritage listed in 2019. It was the first Australian World Heritage place listed only for its Aboriginal cultural values.
rejected.remember: The Gunditjmara engineered channels, weirs and traps to farm eels, and Budj Bim was World Heritage listed in 2019.

a.q: What did the Gunditjmara build at Budj Bim to farm eels?
opts: A system of channels, weirs and traps
A set of dams to store drinking water
A network of canals for boat travel
A row of fish farms with sea cages
a.why: The Gunditjmara changed the flow of water with channels, weirs and traps so eels could be held and caught. The system farmed eels. It was not built to store drinking water or to carry boats.
a.clue: Think about how water was moved and eels were caught.

b.q: A student says the Budj Bim listing shows the Gunditjmara only gathered wild eels. Which reply is best?
opts: They built and managed a system to farm eels
They used fire to drive eels out of the lava
They gathered eels only from the open ocean
They brought eels from other regions to breed
b.why: The channels, weirs and traps show planned management of water and eels over thousands of years, which is aquaculture. Gathering wild eels by chance would not need this built system.
b.clue: Look at what the structures were for.

wants.why: It lets students see how the land was shaped for eel farming.

version.title: Budj Bim and Gunditjmara aquaculture
card: Budj Bim is a volcano in western Victoria, on Gunditjmara Country. Its lava flowed across the land tens of thousands of years ago and shaped a wide area of wetlands.
The Gunditjmara built channels, weirs and traps into the lava rock. These moved water and eels into ponds, where the eels were held and caught when needed.
This is aquaculture: raising and harvesting water animals in a managed system. Parts of the system at Budj Bim are more than 6,000 years old.
A steady supply of eels let families settle in one area, where they built stone huts. The Budj Bim Cultural Landscape was World Heritage listed in 2019.
version.remember: The Gunditjmara shaped the lava wetlands into a managed eel system, now on the World Heritage list.

a.q: Why is the Gunditjmara system at Budj Bim called aquaculture?
opts: Eels were moved, held and harvested in a managed system
Eels were caught by hand wherever they happened to be
Lava flows made wetlands where wild eels could live
Channels drained the wetlands to make dry land for crops
a.why: Aquaculture means raising and harvesting water animals in a managed system, and the channels, weirs and traps moved, held and caught eels. The lava flows made the wetlands, but wetlands on their own are not a managed system.
a.clue: What makes farming different from just finding food?

b.q: At Budj Bim, visitors can see stone eel traps and, close by, the stone bases of old huts. What do these two together suggest?
opts: A reliable eel supply let families settle in one area
Families moved on once the eels in an area ran out
The channels drained the wetland so huts could be built
Eels were scarce, so people relied mostly on hunting
b.why: The traps gave a steady supply of eels, so families could stay in one area and build stone huts to live in. Moving on when the eels ran out is tempting, but the system was built to keep eels coming.
b.clue: Why would people build stone huts next to a food source?

wants.brief: A photo of a stone channel or weir built into the lava rock at Budj Bim in western Victoria, with water flowing through it.
wants.why: Students can see how the Gunditjmara shaped the lava rock to move water and eels.

a.best: Eels were moved, held and harvested in a managed system

b.best: A reliable eel supply let families settle in one area

check.summary: No problems found. The facts on Budj Bim's lava flow, the eel traps more than 6,000 years old, the stone huts and the 2019 World Heritage listing check out, but the point is about Gunditjmara culture, so it needs the owner's review.
